all.text: Click on a door

The thousands of people here answered a question about the afterlife as part of the [Global Flourishing Study](https://globalflourishingstudy.com/). Keep walking!
Scroll to walk

As you explore, you can click on a person to learn more about them.
Click on a person

Here in the front are younger people. As you walk to the back, you’ll encounter older people.
Click the minimap
Young people are most likely to have malleable beliefs about the afterlife. Between the two rounds of surveys, 18 months apart, lots of people in this part of the room changed their answer.
Here’s who changed their answer. The most entrenched 20-somethings are people who believe in an afterlife—but even a quarter of that group moved.
>> CHANGE_BELIEF-AGE-LINE
As expected, belief in an afterlife is [closely correlated](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-024-83541-x) to whether they’re affiliated with a religion.

Just as strong of a predictor is whether people say religion is important in their lives. But in [Europe](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/jssr.12901) and the [U.S.](https://academic.oup.com/sf/article/104/1/366/8002178), it’s quite common for young people to believe in an afterlife but say that religion is not important.
>> BELIEF-WITHOUT-RELIGION-LINE | Afterlife believers who say religion isn't important in their lives

Scholars long believed that the rise of science knowledge would create an increasingly secular world. But that [hasn’t been the case](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/sacred-and-secular/5CE209CE245D444D40BB44D0DDD78F43). From the 1980s to mid-2000s, religion exploded—particularly in former Soviet countries, as well as China, Mexico, Brazil, and the U.S.

Since then, religious belief has fallen in most countries—especially in the U.S., but also other wealthier countries. One theory is that when people face constant threats to their lives, religion encourages them to have more children so their community survives. But as life becomes safer, religion fades generation by generation.

Still today, people who have faced a life-threatening situation are more likely to change their afterlife belief. To no one’s surprise, afterlife belief helps some people [cope](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10704099/) with the anxiety of death.
>> CHANGE-THREAT-LINE|Changing afterlife belief, by life-threatening situations experienced
When people hit their 50s, their afterlife beliefs start to solidify, especially for people who regularly attend religious services.
People in their 50s who believe in an afterlife rarely change their answer and cross into the “no” part of the room. This includes people who have never set foot in a religious service.
There are some regional differences. In sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, belief stays high at every age group. But in the U.S. and Europe, older believers get less and less likely to move.
>> CHANGE-ATTEND_SVCS-LINE|Changing afterlife belief, by regular church attendance

People in their 60s who are unsure are more likely to move toward the belief that everyone around them holds. In fact, if they’re skeptics but a regular church attender, they are far more likely to move toward belief.
But people who are frequently depressed continue to change their answers at a higher rate, even late in their lives.
>> CHANGE-DEPRESSED-LINE|Changing afterlife belief, by depression levels
In younger cohorts, being unsure is a sort of “still exploring” signal. But people in their 70s will likely hold this uncertainty for the rest of their life.
At this age, if unsure people change their mind, they are slightly more likely to settle on no afterlife.
>> UNSURE-CHANGE-LINE|WHERE UNSURE PEOPLE MOVE
What we believe probably doesn’t change whether there is an afterlife or not. But exploring this mystery helps us make sense of our lives—and the anxiety of the fact that it will end.
For many of us, knowing that there is something better in the afterlife has helped us cope with the brutal nature of our lives. We often explore this belief together with shared stories and rituals.
For many of us, it’s hard to believe that there’s anything after the end—either because there is no evidence of it, or because our experiences have nudged us to disbelief.

When we encounter people in another part of this room, we sometimes [see them as not one of us](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.paid.2023.112352). After all, if they don’t share our beliefs about the afterlife, doesn’t that mean they live in an entirely different reality than we do?
We come into this world alone—and the unstoppable forces of time push us forward in this room. At the end, we leave this world alone—and we’re cursed to never know what’s on the other side.
But when we’re here, we can move side to side—and explore this huge mystery together.

info:
This piece was made by [Alvin Chang](https://alvinschang.com/) using data from the [Global Flourish Study](https://globalflourishingstudy.com/). The survey data includes nearly 130,000 respondents from 23 countries that completed both waves of the survey in 2022-23 and 2024. The room includes a representative sample of 1,500 respondents. The broad historical and cohort findings are from the [Integrated Values Surveys](https://www.worldvaluessurvey.org/WVSNewsShow.jsp?ID=442), which combines the World Values Survey and the European Values Study. Percentages are included in the charts, but what drives the findings and the overarching story is the broad comparisons and the direction of change.


One thing that isn’t included in this piece is that the worldwide belief and religiosity numbers have stayed relatively steady. Researchers Pippa Norris and Ronald Inglehart have [found](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/sacred-and-secular/5CE209CE245D444D40BB44D0DDD78F43) that this is because of two phenomena that cut against each other: One is that people in wealthier countries faced a decreasing amount of existential threats—and,  in turn, religiosity and fertility rates dropped. The other is that people in poorer countries still face existential threats, and religion continues to provide security and predictability; fertility rates in those countries have stayed high. As a result, belief has stayed steady worldwide, even though belief within countries has changed rapidly.


The two songs are original compositions, named “Sunday” and “Monday,” created in Ableton Live.


To read more about how this piece was made and to keep up with Alvin’s work, subscribe to [this newsletter](https://buttondown.com/charthead/).
